meta.title: Who really said "I took a deep breath and listened to the old brag of my heart: I am, I am, I am"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Sylvia Plath wrote it, in her 1963 novel The Bell Jar (Ch. 20). The novel prints a period, not a colon, before "I am, I am, I am."

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Plath’s only novel, The Bell Jar (1963), near the close of the book (Chapter 20), as the narrator Esther Greenwood listens to her own heartbeat. The line is genuinely hers — though the novel itself prints a period, “the old brag of my heart. I am, I am, I am,” where the popular version substitutes a colon.

Goodreads reproduces it from The Bell Jar with the novel’s period before “I am, I am, I am.”
The passage falls in Chapter 20, as Esther Greenwood waits for her exit interview and hears her own steady heartbeat — an affirmation of survival.
source.excerptNote: As printed in The Bell Jar. The much-shared social-media wording swaps the period for a colon (“…heart: I am, I am, I am”); the words are otherwise exact.

author.name: Sylvia Plath
author.heading: About Sylvia Plath
author.bio: Sylvia Plath was an American poet, novelist, and short-story writer, a leading figure of the confessional-poetry movement. Her semi-autobiographical novel The Bell Jar (1963) and the posthumous collection Ariel (1965) made her one of the most widely read writers of the twentieth century. She died in London in 1963; her Collected Poems won the Pulitzer Prize in 1982.

misattribution.heading: Wording & the record
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Plath. What travels imperfectly is the punctuation.

items.why: The novel prints a full stop: “…the old brag of my heart. I am, I am, I am.” The version most often shared online (and asked about here) uses a colon, “…heart: I am, I am, I am.” The words are exact; only the mark between the clauses differs. See the sourced text.
A mangled form, “the old bray in my heart,” circulates on social media. “Bray” is an error for “brag” — the correct word in every edition of the novel.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Sylvia Plath, from The Bell Jar (1963), Chapter 20 — just quote it with a period, not a colon, per the sourced text.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line comes near the end of The Bell Jar, Plath’s account of a gifted young woman’s breakdown and slow recovery. As Esther Greenwood waits to be discharged, the beat of her own heart — its “old brag” — becomes a plain, physical proof that she is still alive.

Stripped of context it reads as pure affirmation, which is why it lands on tattoos, posters, and Instagram. In the novel the tone is more hard-won: survival stated as a bare fact rather than a triumph.
